source.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
source.authors: Prudhviraj Naidu; Zixian Wang; Leon Bergen; R. Paturi

record.file_problem: The full paper and technical appendix are present. Some figure contents are not available as readable numerical data in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses probing and feature ablation to test whether meaningful algorithmic features develop before observable task-performance gains, a different method from the grokking progress measures described in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports algorithmic-task loss transitions and quiet-feature results. It explicitly distinguishes its single-epoch loss transitions from grokking's transition from memorization to generalization. Its feature-ablation results test whether quiet features matter causally. No results test the dataset-size dependence of grokking delay or the other listed mechanisms and settings.
record.test_reason: Not a test. Models are trained for at most a single epoch, so there is no memorization phase and no train/test gap. The authors say these runs do not show a memorization-to-generalization transition. The quiet-feature probes track progress before a loss phase transition, not before a grokking jump. This is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version rather than V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. Quiet intermediate features are learned during a flat-loss phase and are causally needed for the task. The authors explicitly distinguish this single-epoch setting from grokking's memorization-to-generalization transition.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Transformer++ models on algorithmic sequence-prediction tasks for at most a single epoch, then probes and ablates intermediate features. It does not reproduce the original grokking training setup or measure its train/test accuracy trajectory.
record.method_sensitivity: Quiet-feature emergence differs by task and token position: early positions are reported first for addition, multiplication, and maximum subarray, while later positions are learned first for breadth first search. Ablation effects vary by task, feature, and input size.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal and within-run validation loss stays flat, then drops abruptly, on several algorithmic tasks in single-epoch training, with no memorization phase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-epoch training on algorithmic tasks shows abrupt loss phase transitions that are distinct from grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: Linearly probeable intermediate algorithmic features emerge before the loss transition, and ablating them mostly degrades accuracy more than random ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden, causally relevant feature learning precedes abrupt loss drops in single-epoch algorithmic training, analogous to progress measures for grokking.

record.problems: Feature-probe curves are presented as figures without numerical values in the supplied text. Probes are selected by lowest training loss across layers, and ablation removes a linear probe direction rather than testing a complete circuit. The study is limited to algorithmic tasks and a single-epoch regime; it does not test the full grokking accuracy trajectory.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the claim were left out.

untested.parts: No train-accuracy saturation followed by delayed test generalization. No dependence on dataset size. Training is single-epoch.
No Fourier or generalizing circuit in a grokking run. No removal of memorizing components. No progress measure anticipating a test-accuracy jump after overfitting.
No non-algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
No weight-decay manipulation, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 labels are removed: the setting lacks the overfitting phase that defines grokking, and the authors say so explicitly. The study is relevant as an analogue to progress measures for grokking (Nanda et al.) but is not evidence on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test training accuracy saturation followed much later by a chance-to-near-perfect test-accuracy transition, or whether smaller training sets require more optimization. It explicitly says its single-epoch setting does not show a transition from memorization to generalization.

It probes interpretable intermediate task features and ablates some of them, but does not identify a Fourier algorithm for modular addition, test removal of memorizing components, or show that the features predict a test-accuracy jump. Its main transition measure is task loss.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm interventions are tested.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
No efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking prediction is tested. Use of AdamW alone is not a test of the proposed account.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact explanations.

reader_labels.condition: Quiet-feature probe trajectories before task-loss transitions in addition, multiplication, maximum subarray, and breadth first search; within-run trajectories
reader_labels.reason: The text reports intermediate features emerging before the loss transition, including within individual runs (R9–R13).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Significant quiet-feature ablation effects versus random ablation
reader_labels.reason: Ablating the listed quiet features significantly reduced test accuracy relative to random-direction ablation (R14–R16, R18, R20, R22, R23).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: First-operand features at input size 16 and weaker feature-ablation effects
reader_labels.reason: The study reports no significant difference from random ablation for the first-operand features in addition and multiplication at input size 16; some other effects are smaller (R17, R19, R21, R22).
